title.en: The Seventh Day: The Work Completed

text.en: The skies and the land were completed, and all their array.
In the seventh age the Sky People completed the work they had made; and they ceased in the seventh age from all the work they had made.
The Sky People blessed the seventh age and set it apart, because in it they ceased from all the work which the Sky People had shaped to do.
So the work on the skies and the land was finished, with everything set in order in them.
In the seventh age those who came from the sky brought the work they had been doing to its end, and stopped all their work of making.
They set the seventh age apart and blessed it, as the age in which the whole work of shaping and making came to an end.
The Messages do not comment on this passage; what follows is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

Verse 1 closes the account that began in 1:1: the skies and the land begun there are now finished, “and all their array”. The Hebrew *tseva’am* is the word for a marshalled host, used elsewhere of the sun, moon and stars; here it covers the whole ordered contents of the world.

The verb of verse 2, *vayishbot*, means “he ceased” and marks the end of an activity; the familiar “he rested” is a looser rendering. It comes from the same root as *shabbat*, and Exodus 20:11 grounds the weekly Sabbath in this seventh day of creation.

As in most of Genesis 1, *Elohim* takes singular verbs here, and the Wheel of Heaven translation keeps “he”. The Reading (the Sky People) and the Meaning (those who came from the sky) render the subject in the plural, as the Messages read the word.
The seventh day is also the only day with no closing “evening and morning”.

The Messages state their own rule of selection: “Only the parts of the Bible I am going to translate for you are important. The others, which are merely poetic chatter, I will not speak to you about.” They pass from the creation of humankind (1:26–27) to the garden without quoting the seventh day, and they do not say whether they count these verses among the others.
In the Wheel of Heaven reading, the seventh day marks the close of the creation work on Earth: the making stops, and the account seals the six stages it has described.

The Wheel of Heaven timeline counts the seventh day as an age as well, the Age of Cancer. In that timeline the creation program closes at the end of the sixth age, with the first humans already in the garden; the disclosure, the expulsion and the generations before the Flood fall within the seventh. The second account that begins at verse 4 goes back over the making of the human, the garden and the woman.
The canon defines a creation “day” as about two thousand Earth years but does not mention a seventh day. The Sabbath meaning of the day is left to the text.

title.en: A Second Account: The Human from the Ground

text.en: This is the tale of the skies and the land in their being shaped — on the day the creators made land and skies.

Now no bush of the field was yet on the land, and no herb of the field had yet sprouted — for the creators had not made it rain on the land, and there was no human to work the ground. A stream would rise from the land and water the whole face of the ground.
The creators formed the human, dust from the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and the human became a living being.
Here begins a second account of the skies and the land. It narrows from the whole planet to one territory and to the creators who worked there, whom it calls YHWH-Elohim.
Before the team’s work, the territory had no cultivated plants: no rain had fallen there and there was no human to work the ground, though water welled up from below and soaked the soil.

Then the creators made the human from the matter of the ground and brought him to life. He was the human of the team working in the country now called Israel, and the Messages say of him that “the man created there was the most intelligent”.

Verse 4 is a seam. *Eleh toledot*, “this is the tale” (literally “the begettings”), is the formula that later opens each new section of Genesis (5:1, 6:9, 10:1 and onward). In the same verse the divine name changes: chapter 1 spoke only of *Elohim*, and from here the account says *YHWH-Elohim*. The order of 1:1, “the skies and the land”, also turns into “land and skies” in the second clause.

Mainstream scholarship reads the change as the join between two originally separate creation accounts, the Priestly account of 1:1–2:4a and the account that begins in 2:4b, often called the Yahwist. The second tells the creation in a different order: the human comes first, then the garden, the animals and the woman.
The Messages comment on these chapters in terms of “the team” and “the creators”, and they do not explain the compound name.

The dictated Messages do give their speaker’s name: “My name is Yahweh and I am the president of the council of the eternals” (ETTMTTP 2:50). The Reading and the Meaning still render YHWH-Elohim as the creators, the team at work in this account.

The Meaning follows the Messages and renders YHWH-Elohim as the creators of one team. Read through the canon, the second account narrows from the work of all the teams across the planet (TBWTT 2:25) to the territory of one of them.

Verses 5 and 6 open on a dry land. The plants missing “of the field” are the kind that need rain and tillage, unlike the plants the land brought forth by itself in 1:11–12. The rare word *ed* in verse 6 is often linked with Akkadian *edû*, water that wells up from below; the older rendering “mist” has little support.

The Messages do not comment on these two verses. In the Wheel of Heaven reading they describe the territory before the team began its work there: the plants that depend on tillage wait for the human who will work the ground.

Verse 7 uses a third creation verb, *yatsar*, the potter’s word for shaping clay. *Ha-adam*, “the human”, is formed from *afar*, dust, of *ha-adamah*, the ground; the article shows that *adam* is not yet a personal name. The breath blown into his nostrils is *nishmat chayim*, and the result is a *nefesh chayah*, “living being”, the same phrase that named the animals in chapter 1.

In the Messages’ account, each team created its humans “artificially”, and the team working in the country now called Israel was “one of the most brilliant, if not the most brilliant”: “And the man created there was the most intelligent.”
Read as a compressed report, the potter’s verb and the breath blown into a finished body describe in craft words what the Messages call creating a human artificially.

Raël’s own commentary, which is not part of the dictated Messages, reads the dust in the same way: “You were only matter, dust, and the Elohim made of you living beings capable of dominating matter, in their image”.
The creators planted a garden in Eden, eastward — and there they placed the human they had formed.
The creators caused every tree desirable to the sight and good for food to sprout from the ground — and within the garden, the means of prolonging life and the scientific books.

A river went out from Eden to water the garden; from there it divided and became four head-streams. The first is named Pishon; it is the one encircling all the land of Havilah, where the gold is. The gold of that land is good; there is bdellium and the shoham stone. The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one encircling all the land of Kush. The name of the third river is Hiddekel; it is the one flowing east of Ashur. And the fourth river is the Perat.
The creators took the human and set him in the garden of Eden to work it and to guard it.

The team laid out a garden in Eden, in the east, and placed there the human it had formed. This was the place people call the earthly paradise: the team’s territory in the country now called Israel, which then lay not far from Greece and Turkey on the single continent.

Its plants were the most fragrant, and every tree grew there that was pleasant to see and good to eat from. Within the garden stood the tree of life, which the Messages tie to “a scientific means” of prolonging life, and the tree of knowing good and bad, whose fruit they read as the scientific books the creators kept from the human.

The territory was well watered. A single river rose in Eden, watered the garden and divided into four head-streams, which the account names together with the lands they surround: the Pishon and the gold of Havilah, the Gihon and the land of Kush, the Tigris east of Ashur, and the Euphrates.

The creators set the human in the garden to work it and look after it. There they educated him while keeping him in ignorance of the great scientific secrets, so that the created would not surpass the creator and his intelligence could be measured.

The Messages introduce the garden with the words “There, the problems began for us.” The team in the country now called Israel, which then lay “not very far from Greece and Turkey on the single continent”, was one of the most brilliant. Its animals were the most beautiful and its plants the most fragrant: “It was what you call the earthly paradise.”
When the Messages reach the expulsion (Genesis 3:24), the guards are placed “at the entrance to the creators’ residence”.

In verse 8 the Hebrew says “a garden in Eden”: Eden is a region, and the garden lies within it. From verse 15 the text also says “the garden of Eden” (*gan-eden*). *Miqedem* usually means “in the east”, but it can also mean “of old”.
The tree of knowing good and bad uses *da’at*, knowing by experience. The pair “good and bad” is often read as a merism, a Hebrew way of saying “everything in the range”.

The Messages read eating from the tree of knowledge as touching “the scientific books” (see 2:16–17). Commenting on Genesis 3:22, they set beside the tree of life the statement that “there is a scientific means” of prolonging human lives “for a very long time”; later, they say, the chiefs of the first men were granted the benefit of the “tree of life”, which is why Adam, Seth and Enosh lived so long.

Two of the four rivers can be identified: *Hiddekel* is the Tigris and *Perat* the Euphrates. The Pishon and the Gihon are unknown, although Havilah and Kush are lands named elsewhere in the Bible, and Gihon is also the name of the spring of Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:33).
The Messages do not comment on the rivers. They place the earthly paradise in the country now called Israel, while the Tigris and Euphrates point to Mesopotamia.
The Wheel of Heaven reading does not try to solve the rivers as a map or to place Eden at a modern site.

The canon places the territory on “the single continent” of that time. One Wheel of Heaven reading takes this to mean that the rivers of verses 10–14 need not match a modern map. The canon does not draw that conclusion.
In verse 15 the human is set in the garden *le-ovdah ul-shomrah*, “to work it and to guard it”: he is the garden’s worker and watchman.

In the Messages, the team’s measures concern the man’s education: “So they had to take measures so that the created would not surpass the creator. He had to be confined in ignorance of the great scientific secrets while being educated, so that his intelligence could be measured.”
Setting these measures beside verse 15 is a Wheel of Heaven reading. The Messages state them of the garden as a whole and go on at once to the prohibition of 2:16–17.
The creators commanded the human, saying, "From every tree of the garden you may freely eat;
but from the scientific books — you shall not eat from them. For on the day you eat from them, you shall surely die."
The creators told the human that he could learn everything he wanted and read all the books they had placed at his disposal.
Only the scientific books he was not to touch: if he did, he would die.

The Messages quote these two verses whole and explain them at once: “Which means: you may learn everything you want, read all the books we have here at your disposal, but do not touch the scientific books or you will die.”
Elsewhere, commenting on Ezekiel’s eating of a scroll, they call eating from this tree an image: “It is in fact a matter of intellectual «food».”

The Messages quote the two verses in French, where the tree is « l’arbre de la science du bien et du mal ». The rendering goes back through the Vulgate’s *lignum scientiae boni et mali* and uses *science* in its older sense of knowledge; the Hebrew *da’at* means knowing.

Permission and prohibition are framed in matching grammar: *akhol tokhel*, “you may freely eat”, and *mot tamut*, “you shall surely die”, both use the emphatic infinitive. Every tree is given, and one is withheld.
The construction makes the consequence certain but leaves its kind open. In the story that follows the human does not die that day.
The Messages repeat the warning in its own terms, “or you will die”, and do not say what kind of death is meant. What followed the disclosure of the knowledge is told in Genesis 3.
The creators said, "It is not good for the human to be alone — I will make for him a counterpart fitting him."

The creators formed from the ground every wild animal of the field and every bird of the skies, and brought them to the human to see what he would call them; and whatever the human called each living being, that became its name.
The human gave names to all the cattle, to the birds of the skies, and to every wild animal of the field — but for the human himself no counterpart fitting him was found.
The creators judged that it was not good for the human to be alone, and resolved to make him a counterpart of matching standing.

Wild animals and birds, also shaped from the ground, were brought to the human to see what he would call them, and whatever he called each one became its name. The creators taught him the name and the powers of everything that lived around him.

He had to know the plants and animals around him well, their way of life and how to get food from them: botany and zoology, knowledge that was no danger to the creators. But among all the animals there was none that could stand beside him as his equal.
The Messages do not comment on verse 18; what follows on it is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

“Not good” is the only negative verdict in the creation accounts. The remedy is an *ezer kenegdo*: *ezer* is substantial help, the same word used of divine help in the Psalms, and *kenegdo* means “corresponding to him”, face to face. The phrase describes a counterpart of matching standing; the old English “helpmeet” fuses the King James Version’s “an help meet for him” into one word.

Read through the canon, the remark is the creators’ own judgement on work still in progress: one human alone was not the finished result, and the Messages later speak of the team’s “two children, male and female”.

The Messages quote verse 19, “And brought them unto the man to see what he would call them”, and explain: he had to know well the plants and animals around him, their way of life and the means of obtaining food through them. “The creators taught him the name and the powers of everything that lived around him: botany and zoology, because that was not dangerous for them.”

The two accounts differ. In Genesis the human gives the names and they stand; in the Messages’ comment the creators teach him the names. The Messages also quote only the middle of the verse. They leave out the forming of the animals, which here follows the human’s, while Genesis 1 and the Messages’ own creation account (TBWTT 2:23–25) put the animals before humankind; and they leave out the closing clause, “whatever the human called each living being, that became its name”.

The two can be read together: the creators bring the animals so that the human learns them, and watching “what he would call them” is a way to measure his intelligence, as the Messages say the team intended.
Verse 20 completes the naming and records the lack: among cattle, birds and wild animals no counterpart fitting the human was found. The failed search leads into the making of the woman.
The creators caused a deep sleep to fall upon the human, and while he slept, they took one of his sides and closed up the flesh in its place.
The creators built the side they had taken from the human into a woman, and brought her to the human.
The human said, "This one at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh — this one shall be called *Ishah* [Woman], for from *Ish* [Man] this one was taken."
Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
The two of them were naked, the human and his woman, and they felt no shame.
The creators put the human into a deep, induced sleep, took one of his sides and closed the flesh over the place.
From what they had taken they built a woman and brought her to him. The team now had two humans in its care, male and female.
The human recognised her as his own kind, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”, and named her woman, *ishah*, because she was taken from man, *ish*.
The account adds a saying of its own: this is why a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
The two of them went naked and felt no shame: they were still children in the team’s care.

The Messages’ only counterpart to this passage is one image: “Imagine the joy of this team of scientists having two children, male and female, running about their legs, to whom they taught all sorts of things they were eager to learn.” Later they name the pair Adam and Eve.
The Messages do not comment on the making of the woman, on the saying about marriage or on the pair’s nakedness; what follows is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

*Tardemah* is not ordinary sleep but a deep sleep brought on from outside; the same word falls on Abram in Genesis 15:12. *Tsela*, traditionally “rib”, names the side of a structure elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, such as the sides of the ark of the covenant or the side chambers of the Temple; the Wheel of Heaven translation renders it “side”. The verb of verse 22 is *banah*, “to build”, the word used for cities, altars and houses.

Read as a compressed report of the creators’ work, an induced sleep, an opened side closed again with flesh, and a woman “built” from what was taken describe an operation under anaesthesia, with the second human made from material of the first. Nothing in the canon states this. The Messages’ own image is of a pair, male and female, raised together.
The human’s words in verse 23 are a naming, like the namings of verses 19–20. The play on *ish* and *ishah* works by sound: the two words come from different roots.
Verse 24 steps outside the story. Neither YHWH-Elohim nor the human speaks; the narrator explains a custom, marriage, as the rejoining of what was divided: the two “become one flesh”.
Read through the canon, which says the biblical text “became laden with mystical and useless phrases over the millennia” (TBWTT 2:3), the aside is the voice of those who handed the record down.
*Arummim*, “naked”, in verse 25 sounds like *arum*, “shrewd”, the word that introduces the serpent in 3:1. The chapter ends with the two unashamed and the serpent not yet named.

Read with the canon, the two are still children in the team’s care. The Messages quote Genesis 3:7, where their eyes are opened and they know they are naked, at the point where the pair, by then “almost adults”, are offered scientific knowledge.
